intro: In this college you'll learn the warm everyday Dutch of small talk: asking how someone is, chatting about the weather, greeting people you already know, inviting someone over, and congratulating them.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — the art of small talk
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme three. Its title is [[Hoe gaat het?]], which means 'How are you?'. This is the theme of small talk, and small talk is the glue of daily life in the Netherlands. When you pass a neighbour on the stairs, when you arrive at work, or when you wait at the school gate, people exchange a few warm words. You do not need long sentences; you need the right little phrases. The most important question of all is [[Hoe gaat het met je?]], the friendly way to ask how someone is doing. To an official or an older person you would politely say [[Hoe gaat het met u?]] instead. And the easy answer everyone uses is [[Het gaat goed, dank je.]], meaning 'It is going well, thank you.' Then you bounce the question back with [[En met jou?]], which means 'And you?'. Remember, in this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence you hear is spoken by a native voice, so you train your ear at the same time. Please repeat each phrase out loud after me. Are you ready? Then let's begin: [[Hoe gaat het met je?]]

paragraphs.heading: How are you? — the full exchange
paragraphs.text: Let's build the whole little exchange, because it always follows the same friendly pattern. Someone asks [[Hoe gaat het met je?]], and you have three easy answers depending on your mood. If life is good, say [[Het gaat goed.]], 'It is going well.' If you feel wonderful, you can say [[Heel goed!]], meaning 'Very good!'. And if you feel just okay, the honest middle answer is [[Het gaat wel.]], a lovely Dutch phrase that means 'so-so' or 'I'm alright'. Notice the grammar hiding here: [[het gaat]] is the simple present tense, literally 'it goes'. Dutch keeps the present tense beautifully simple, with no extra '-ing' form, so [[het gaat goed]] covers both 'it goes well' and 'it is going well'. After you answer, always return the question with [[En met jou?]], or politely [[En met u?]]. A very Dutch touch is the warm little word [[hoor]], as in [[Goed hoor, dank je.]] — it adds a friendly, reassuring tone, like 'Oh, I'm fine, thanks.' Practise the full round now: [[Hoe gaat het met je?]] ... [[Goed hoor, dank je. En met jou?]] That short loop will serve you every single day.

paragraphs.heading: The weather — the national small-talk topic
paragraphs.text: Now we reach a true Dutch obsession: the weather, which is [[het weer]]. The Dutch talk about [[het weer]] constantly, and a comment about it is the safest way in the world to start a conversation with anyone. The classic opener is [[Lekker weertje, hè?]], meaning 'Nice weather, isn't it?'. That little word [[hè]] at the end invites the other person to agree, exactly like the English 'isn't it?'. Let's gather the key words. The sun is [[de zon]], the rain is [[de regen]], the wind is [[de wind]], and snow is [[de sneeuw]]. To describe the day, the two everyday adjectives are [[warm]], meaning 'warm', and [[koud]], meaning 'cold'. So on a cold morning you might exclaim [[Wat is het koud vandaag!]], 'How cold it is today!'. On a grey day, the Dutch enjoy a colourful saying: [[Het regent pijpenstelen.]], which literally means 'it is raining pipe stems' and is their version of 'raining cats and dogs'. And there is a hopeful proverb too: [[Na regen komt zonneschijn.]], 'after rain comes sunshine', a gentle way of saying better times will come. Try one out tomorrow with a neighbour.

paragraphs.heading: Greeting people you know
paragraphs.text: Small talk really begins the moment you greet someone, so let's gather warm greetings for people you already know. The time-of-day greetings are still your foundation: [[Goedemorgen]] in the morning, [[Goedemiddag]] in the afternoon, and [[Goedenavond]] in the evening. With friends and neighbours a casual [[Hoi]] or [[Hallo]] is perfect any time. But here is the phrase that makes people smile: when you run into someone you have not seen for a while, say [[Leuk je weer te zien!]], which means 'Nice to see you again!'. This is warmer than a plain hello, and it tells the other person you are genuinely glad. To ask question words naturally, learn the small set the Dutch use most: [[wie]] means 'who', [[wat]] means 'what', [[waar]] means 'where', [[hoe]] means 'how', and [[wanneer]] means 'when'. So you might warmly ask an old friend [[Hoe gaat het nu met je?]], 'How are you doing now?', or [[Waar woon je tegenwoordig?]], 'Where do you live these days?'. When you part, a lovely closing is [[Tot de volgende keer!]], meaning 'Until next time!'. And to send your regards onward, say [[Doe de groeten aan je vrouw.]], 'Say hello to your wife.'

paragraphs.heading: Inviting someone over and making plans
paragraphs.text: Once you are chatting warmly, the natural next step is an invitation, which in Dutch is [[de uitnodiging]]. The Dutch love a cosy, sociable get-together, and they have a famous word for that warm atmosphere: [[gezellig]]. There is no perfect English translation, but it means cosy, friendly, and pleasant all at once. To invite a friend, the easy phrase is [[Heb je zin om langs te komen?]], which means 'Do you feel like dropping by?'. That handy expression [[zin hebben]] means 'to feel like' doing something. Even simpler and very common is [[Kom je vanavond koffiedrinken?]], meaning 'Are you coming over for coffee tonight?', because coffee is the heart of Dutch hospitality. To set the time you ask [[Hoe laat?]], meaning 'What time?', and to fix a plan you might say [[Kom om acht uur.]], 'Come at eight o'clock.' When the other person accepts, the warm reaction is [[Wat leuk!]], 'How nice!', or [[Wat gezellig!]], 'How cosy!'. As they leave you wish them [[Veel plezier!]], meaning 'Have fun!'. And if someone sadly cannot come, you respond kindly with [[Jammer dat je niet kunt komen.]], 'A pity that you cannot come.' These few lines turn a chat into a real friendship.

paragraphs.heading: Congratulations — and putting it all together
paragraphs.text: The last warm skill of this theme is congratulating people, and the magic word is [[Gefeliciteerd!]], meaning 'Congratulations!'. The Dutch celebrate the birthday, [[de verjaardag]], very seriously, often with a little party, [[een feestje]], and a small present, [[een cadeautje]]. To be specific you say [[Gefeliciteerd met je verjaardag!]], 'Congratulations on your birthday!'. When someone shares happy news, [[het nieuws]], a lovely reaction is [[Wat fijn voor je!]], 'How nice for you!'. And if a friend is unwell, you wish them [[Beterschap!]], meaning 'Get well soon!'. Now let's put everything together in a real mini-scene. You meet your neighbour outside: [[Hoi! Leuk je weer te zien. Hoe gaat het met je?]] He answers, [[Goed hoor, dank je. Lekker weertje, hè?]] You agree, then he says it is his birthday this weekend, so you smile and say [[O, gefeliciteerd! Doe je iets leuks?]] He invites you with [[Kom je langs voor koffie?]], and you happily reply [[Wat leuk, heel graag!]] Do you see how small the words are, yet how warm the moment becomes? Practise this out loud today. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — and I will see you in theme four!
